R Graphics: Base R vs. lattice vs. ggplot2

Side-by-side code and figure comparisons

1 How to use this handout

This handout compares the same plot type in three graphics systems. In each row, the code appears directly above its plot. The data, grouping variables, histogram breaks, and (for the confidence-band example) model predictions are shared so that the comparison is as fair as possible.

  1. Open this .Rmd file in RStudio.
  2. Install the required packages once, if needed: install.packages(c("lattice", "ggplot2", "rmarkdown")).
  3. Click Knit and choose HTML. No external data downloads are needed.

Key idea: Base R uses plotting functions and adds layers to an existing plot. lattice emphasizes formula syntax and conditional plots. ggplot2 builds plots by combining layers with +.

2 1. Scatterplot

Question: Is vehicle weight associated with fuel economy?

2.1 Base R

plot(mpg ~ wt, data = cars,
     pch = 16, col = point_col,
     xlab = "Weight (1,000 lbs)",
     ylab = "Miles per gallon")

2.2 lattice

xyplot(mpg ~ wt, data = cars,
       pch = 16, col = point_col,
       xlab = "Weight (1,000 lbs)",
       ylab = "Miles per gallon")

2.3 ggplot2

ggplot(cars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point(color = point_col) +
  labs(x = "Weight (1,000 lbs)",
       y = "Miles per gallon")

3 2. Scatterplot with groups and a legend

The cyl variable was explicitly converted to a factor: we want categories, not a continuous color scale.

3.1 Base R

plot(mpg ~ wt, data = cars,
     pch = 16,
     col = cyl_cols[as.character(cars$cyl)],
     xlab = "Weight", ylab = "MPG")
legend("topright", legend = levels(cars$cyl),
       col = cyl_cols, pch = 16,
       title = "Cylinders", bty = "n")

3.2 lattice

xyplot(mpg ~ wt, data = cars,
       groups = cyl, pch = 16,
       xlab = "Weight", ylab = "MPG",
       par.settings = list(
         superpose.symbol = list(
           col = unname(cyl_cols), pch = 16)),
       auto.key = list(space = "top",
                       columns = 3,
                       title = "Cylinders"))

3.3 ggplot2

ggplot(cars, aes(wt, mpg, color = cyl)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_manual(values = cyl_cols) +
  labs(x = "Weight", y = "MPG",
       color = "Cylinders") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

4 3. Scatterplot with a logarithmic x-axis

All three plots use a base-10 logarithmic x-axis. Only the axis changes; the dataset remains unchanged.

4.1 Base R

plot(mpg ~ disp, data = cars,
     log = "x", pch = 16, col = point_col,
     xlab = "Displacement (log10 axis)",
     ylab = "MPG")

4.2 lattice

xyplot(mpg ~ disp, data = cars,
       pch = 16, col = point_col,
       scales = list(x = list(
         log = 10, equispaced.log = FALSE)),
       xlab = "Displacement (log10 axis)",
       ylab = "MPG")

4.3 ggplot2

ggplot(cars, aes(disp, mpg)) +
  geom_point(color = point_col) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Displacement (log10 axis)",
       y = "MPG")

5 4. Histogram

The same bin boundaries (10, 15, ..., 35) and counts, not percentages or densities, are used throughout. Histograms describe a continuous distribution; unlike bar charts, their x-axis represents a numeric scale.

5.1 Base R

hist(cars$mpg, breaks = hist_breaks,
     col = bar_col, border = "white",
     main = "", xlab = "MPG",
     ylab = "Count")

5.2 lattice

histogram(~ mpg, data = cars,
          breaks = hist_breaks,
          type = "count",
          col = bar_col, border = "white",
          xlab = "MPG", ylab = "Count")

5.3 ggplot2

ggplot(cars, aes(mpg)) +
  geom_histogram(breaks = hist_breaks,
                 fill = bar_col,
                 color = "white") +
  labs(x = "MPG", y = "Count")

6 5. Density curve

Density plots show a smoothed estimate of the distribution. Here the bandwidth is fixed at 2 in all three implementations.

6.1 Base R

plot(density(cars$mpg, bw = 2),
     col = point_col, lwd = 2,
     main = "", xlab = "MPG",
     ylab = "Density")

6.2 lattice

densityplot(~ mpg, data = cars,
            bw = 2, plot.points = FALSE,
            col = point_col, lwd = 2,
            xlab = "MPG", ylab = "Density")

6.3 ggplot2

ggplot(cars, aes(mpg)) +
  geom_density(bw = 2,
               color = point_col,
               linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "MPG", y = "Density")

7 6. Boxplot by group

All three are vertical boxplots with the same categorical x-axis. A numeric variable such as cyl should be converted into a factor before grouping.

7.1 Base R

boxplot(mpg ~ cyl, data = cars,
        col = bar_col,
        xlab = "Cylinders", ylab = "MPG")

7.2 lattice

bwplot(mpg ~ cyl, data = cars,
       fill = bar_col,
       xlab = "Cylinders", ylab = "MPG")

7.3 ggplot2

ggplot(cars, aes(cyl, mpg)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = bar_col) +
  labs(x = "Cylinders", y = "MPG")

8 7. Observations plus a linear regression line

The linear model is mpg ~ wt. The line represents the estimated conditional mean, not individual predicted outcomes.

8.1 Base R

plot(mpg ~ wt, data = cars,
     pch = 16, col = point_col,
     xlab = "Weight", ylab = "MPG")
abline(fit, col = fit_col, lwd = 2)

8.2 lattice

xyplot(mpg ~ wt, data = cars,
       type = c("p", "r"),
       pch = 16, col = point_col,
       col.line = fit_col, lwd = 2,
       xlab = "Weight", ylab = "MPG")

8.3 ggplot2

ggplot(cars, aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_point(color = point_col) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x,
              se = FALSE, color = fit_col) +
  labs(x = "Weight", y = "MPG")

9 8. Observations, fitted line, and 95% confidence band

Important distinction: The shaded region is the pointwise 95% confidence interval for the conditional mean \(E(\mathrm{MPG}\mid\mathrm{weight})\). It is not a 95% prediction interval for an individual car and not a simultaneous confidence band. The same fitted values and confidence limits from predict(..., interval = "confidence") are used in all three plots.

9.1 Base R

plot(mpg ~ wt, data = cars, type = "n",
     xlab = "Weight", ylab = "MPG")
polygon(c(pred$wt, rev(pred$wt)),
        c(pred$lwr, rev(pred$upr)),
        col = adjustcolor(band_col, alpha.f = 0.5),
        border = NA)
points(mpg ~ wt, data = cars,
       pch = 16, col = point_col)
lines(pred$wt, pred$fit,
      col = fit_col, lwd = 2)

9.2 lattice

xyplot(mpg ~ wt, data = cars,
       xlab = "Weight", ylab = "MPG",
       panel = function(x, y, ...) {
         panel.polygon(
           c(pred$wt, rev(pred$wt)),
           c(pred$lwr, rev(pred$upr)),
           col = adjustcolor(band_col,
                             alpha.f = 0.5),
           border = NA)
         panel.xyplot(x, y, pch = 16,
                      col = point_col, ...)
         panel.lines(pred$wt, pred$fit,
                     col = fit_col, lwd = 2)
       })

9.3 ggplot2

ggplot(cars, aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = pred,
    aes(x = wt, ymin = lwr, ymax = upr),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    fill = band_col, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_point(color = point_col) +
  geom_line(data = pred, aes(x = wt, y = fit),
            inherit.aes = FALSE,
            color = fit_col, linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Weight", y = "MPG")

Teaching alternative: In ggplot2, geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) creates a fitted line and 95% confidence band more concisely. The longer version above makes the identical numerical inputs explicit across all three plotting systems.

10 9. Bar chart of category counts

All three use the same pre-aggregated count table (counts). In ggplot2, geom_col() plots existing heights; geom_bar() counts observations in raw data.

10.1 Base R

barplot(counts$n,
        names.arg = counts$cyl,
        col = bar_col,
        xlab = "Cylinders", ylab = "Count")

10.2 lattice

barchart(n ~ cyl, data = counts,
         horizontal = FALSE,
         col = bar_col,
         xlab = "Cylinders", ylab = "Count")

10.3 ggplot2

ggplot(counts, aes(cyl, n)) +
  geom_col(fill = bar_col) +
  labs(x = "Cylinders", y = "Count")

11 10. Line plot

The first 12 monthly observations from the built-in AirPassengers dataset are used in every column.

11.1 Base R

plot(passengers ~ month, data = air_df,
     type = "b", pch = 16, col = point_col,
     xlab = "Month (1949)",
     ylab = "Passengers (thousands)")

11.2 lattice

xyplot(passengers ~ month, data = air_df,
       type = "b", pch = 16,
       col = point_col,
       xlab = "Month (1949)",
       ylab = "Passengers (thousands)")

11.3 ggplot2

ggplot(air_df, aes(month, passengers)) +
  geom_line(color = point_col) +
  geom_point(color = point_col) +
  labs(x = "Month (1949)",
       y = "Passengers (thousands)")

12 11. Small multiples (conditioning / faceting)

Compare separate panels by transmission type while keeping the same x- and y-axis ranges. Base R needs an explicit loop; lattice and ggplot2 have built-in faceting syntax.

12.1 Base R

oldpar <- par(mfrow = c(2, 1),
              mar = c(3.4, 3.5, 1.6, 0.6))
for (g in levels(cars$am)) {
  d <- subset(cars, am == g)
  plot(mpg ~ wt, data = d,
       xlim = range(cars$wt),
       ylim = range(cars$mpg),
       pch = 16, col = point_col,
       main = g, xlab = "Weight",
       ylab = "MPG")
}

par(oldpar)

12.2 lattice

xyplot(mpg ~ wt | am, data = cars,
       layout = c(1, 2),
       pch = 16, col = point_col,
       xlab = "Weight", ylab = "MPG")

12.3 ggplot2

ggplot(cars, aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_point(color = point_col) +
  facet_wrap(~ am, ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "Weight", y = "MPG")

13 12. Scatterplot with a nonlinear smoother (optional)

These are similar smoothing ideas, but not necessarily identical numerical algorithms: Base R uses lowess(), while the other interfaces use LOESS. Compare the modeling assumptions rather than treating the curves as mathematically identical.

13.1 Base R

plot(mpg ~ wt, data = cars,
     pch = 16, col = point_col,
     xlab = "Weight", ylab = "MPG")
lines(lowess(cars$wt, cars$mpg),
      col = fit_col, lwd = 2)

13.2 lattice

xyplot(mpg ~ wt, data = cars,
       type = c("p", "smooth"),
       pch = 16, col = point_col,
       col.line = fit_col, lwd = 2,
       xlab = "Weight", ylab = "MPG")

13.3 ggplot2

ggplot(cars, aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_point(color = point_col) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess",
              formula = y ~ x,
              se = FALSE, color = fit_col) +
  labs(x = "Weight", y = "MPG")

14 Summary: which syntax should students remember?

Task Base R lattice ggplot2
Scatterplot plot(y ~ x, data = d) xyplot(y ~ x, data = d) ggplot(d, aes(x, y)) + geom_point()
Histogram hist(d$x) histogram(~ x, data = d) ggplot(d, aes(x)) + geom_histogram()
Boxplot boxplot(y ~ group, data = d) bwplot(y ~ group, data = d) ggplot(d, aes(group, y)) + geom_boxplot()
Linear regression line abline(lm(y ~ x, data = d)) xyplot(..., type = c("p", "r")) geom_smooth(method = "lm")
Separate panels par(mfrow = ...); for (...) xyplot(y ~ x \| group, ...) facet_wrap(~ group)
Add another element points(), lines(), polygon() panel.points(), panel.lines(), etc. Add another geom_*() layer

14.1 Points for discussion

  • Base R: imperative approach. Each successive command adds to the current plot; simple plots are concise.
  • lattice: formula-driven approach. Conditioning (| group) and grouping are integral to the system; returned objects are trellis plots.
  • ggplot2: layered grammar. Data, aesthetics, geometric elements, scales, and facets are separate components.
  • A fair comparison requires controlled settings. For histograms, match the breaks and y-axis metric; for boxplots, match grouping and orientation; for modeled curves, match the model and interval definition.
  • A confidence interval is not a prediction interval. An individual prediction interval would be wider than the pointwise confidence interval for the expected response.

Teaching note: All displayed code uses standard R datasets. The cross-column layout is optimized for desktop browsers and landscape printouts; on narrow screens, columns stack vertically.
